To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

ALS-motor patients show GM volume reduction in frontal and cerebello-cerebral regions, while ALS-plus show a more diffuse reduction in primary motor and fronto-temporal regions, cerebellum, basal ganglia and precuneus, and that ALS-plus patients also present with WM alterations in motor and non-motor tracts, while ALS-motor show WM abnormalities in motor and extra-moral tracts.

we found that patients with amyotrophic lateral slerosis (ALS), a motor system disorder, have widespread structural changes in gray and white matter in both motor and extra-motorsystems, even in patients without cognitive deficits.

non-demented ALS patients with cognitive impairment (ALS-plus) show diffuse gray matter atrophy and white matter abnormalities beyond the motor system and corticospital tract, while ALS patients with no cognitive impairment (ALS motor) show gray matter changes within and beyond the motor system, and white matter changes within the motor system.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the present study demonstrates that non-demented ALS patients have widespread brain changes, including the motor system, the frontotemporal network, the corpus callosal fibers and the cerebellum, which may be associated with cognitive and behavioral impairment.
ALS-plus patients show more widespread GM and WM changes than ALS-motor patients.
we found GM changes in motor and extra-motors areas, and WM changes in motor and several extra-motor tractors in ALS-plus patients compared to ALS-motor patients and HC.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the motor cortex and its tracts are not the only areas affected in ALS, and that ALS patients with cognitive impairment have more extensive brain changes than patients without cognitive impairment, even if frank cognitive impairment is not detected.
cognitive impairment in ALS patients is not a simple consequence of motor system degeneration.
